title: Wildfires and the way we manage forests

turns.speaker: Talia
turns.text: Another record season. And every article says climate change, full stop, as though that's the whole explanation.

turns.speaker: Jens
turns.text: It's a large part of it. Hotter, drier, longer seasons, that's measurable.

turns.speaker: Rowan
turns.text: It's necessary and not sufficient. The other half is a century of putting every fire out the moment it started.

turns.speaker: Rowan
turns.text: Enormously. These forests used to burn lightly every decade or so and clear the undergrowth. Stop that and you get one fire that takes the canopy.

turns.speaker: Jens
turns.text: Which is why controlled burning keeps coming up, and keeps not happening at scale.

turns.speaker: Talia
turns.text: Because the window is narrow and the risk is asymmetric. Nobody was ever fired for not lighting a fire.

turns.speaker: Talia
turns.text: If your burn escapes, that's your career. If you skip it, the fire arrives in someone else's term.

turns.speaker: Rowan
turns.text: That's the institutional problem in one sentence.

turns.speaker: Jens
turns.text: Indigenous fire management did this for thousands of years and is finally being brought back in a few places.

turns.speaker: Rowan
turns.text: Slowly, and with the liability question unresolved.

turns.speaker: Talia
turns.text: There's also the building. Half the losses are houses put in forest with wooden decks and no clearance.

turns.speaker: Jens
turns.text: Which is a planning decision, not a climate one, and much easier to change.

points: Record wildfire seasons are commonly attributed solely to climate change.
Rowan argues climate is necessary but not sufficient, with a century of fire suppression allowing fuel to accumulate.
Forests that once burned lightly every decade now carry enough fuel for canopy-destroying fires.
Controlled burning is rarely done at scale because risk is asymmetric: an escaped burn ends a career while inaction defers the consequence.
Indigenous fire management is being reintroduced slowly, with liability unresolved.
Talia notes many losses involve houses built in forest without clearance, which is a planning decision and easier to change.
